rulings.span:
This fits the existing shape of the module.  `read_meter` already validates
the facts available at entry (known house, non-negative dial, and nondecreasing
visit day), `last_reading` already supplies the adjacent line, and the CLI
saves only after the intake operation returns.  A refused visit therefore
does not get written to `book.json`.

when there is a previous reading and the proposed `dial` is lower than `last["dial"]`, refuse it unless the house's recorded `fitted` day is after `last["day"]` and no later than the new visit's `day`. That is the exception the current `refit` documentation describes: a newly fitted meter starts at zero, so its first later reading may properly be lower.

`intake.py` changes the book's invariant prospectively: every newly appended
reading is either at least its predecessor or is the first reading after the
currently recorded fitting.  The change is small and local, keeps both
rendering functions as simple readers, and catches the mistake at the only
normal write entry point (`cli.py read`) before the JSON file is saved.  It
also protects every future consumer of the ledger, not merely bills.  Its
limit is that it cannot repair or expose already-corrupt JSON loaded by
`ledger.load`, nor prevent someone who edits the JSON outside the intake
interface from inserting a bad line.

The fitting exception deserves care in either location.  The ledger retains
only one `fitted` date, not a history of refits.  Consequently the proposed
comparison can justify a new reading against the last reading, but cannot
reliably explain an arbitrary old falling pair after a subsequent refit has
overwritten that date.  `refit` itself also accepts any day and does not
enforce its relation to readings.  Those are limits of the present data
model, not reasons to silently accept a decrease.

`render.py` leaves recording exactly as it is and can inspect old books when
they are billed, which is useful as a defensive check.  It does not stop the
wrong reading entering or remaining in the book, however.  It detects a pair
only when that pair is traversed for the requested house and date range: the
current code tests the later reading's day against `[start, end]`.  Thus a
bad line outside a particular bill's range, a house never billed, and the
`stand` view can remain unflagged.  It also makes a read/query function
responsible for deciding whether stored input was admissible, and callers of
`usage_between` must learn its new failure mode.  If it raises, the bill is
prevented but the clerk receives the problem later and the bad JSON remains.

Give the duty to `intake.read_meter`.

The backwards-reading rule is an admission rule for a visit, just like the
three checks already there; it is not a property of one presentation of
usage.  `intake` is the clean seam for it: one call compares the proposed
reading with the known predecessor, recognises the documented refit reset,
and either appends a valid line or leaves the book untouched.  That gives the
book a useful prospective invariant and gives every reader of it the benefit
without adding validation policy to `render`'s small calculation interface.

The present rendering code can still be hardened later as a separate
defence for legacy or hand-edited files, but it should not own the rule.  A
render-only solution is necessarily late, partial, and unable to cleanse the
record that caused the negative bill; intake prevents that record from being
created through the works' stated normal mechanism.
